decision.explanation: Rationalizing gives (√(x+4)−2)/x = 1/(√(x+4)+2) for x ≠ 0. As x approaches 0, this approaches 1/(2+2) = 1/4.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & =\frac{\sqrt{0+4}-2}{0}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\sqrt{x+4}-2)(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x+4-4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{0+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Multiply by the conjugate to obtain 2/(√(2x−7)+1) for x ≠ 4. Taking x → 4 gives 2/(1+1) = 1.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{2x-7}-1}{x-4} & =\frac{\sqrt{2(4)-7}-1}{4-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{2x-7}-1}{x-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{(\sqrt{2x-7}-1)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{{(\sqrt{2x-7})}^{2}-{1}^{2}}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2x-7-1}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2x-8}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2(x-4)}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2x-7}+1} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2(4)-7}+1} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
